Pain exacerbated by rotational weight-bearing (e.g., pivoting, squatting, twisting) reflects mechanical impingement or displacement of a torn meniscal fragment. The absence of effusion, swelling, warmth, or erythema argues strongly against septic arthritis, inflammatory arthropathy, or acute hemarthrosis (which would typically accompany more severe ligamentous injury like ACL tear). Negative plain radiographs appropriately rule out bony pathology (fracture, dislocation, osteochondral lesion large enough to be radiographically apparent), further narrowing the differential to soft-tissue intra-articular injury. The recommendation for MRI—not ultrasound or repeat X-ray—is evidence-based: MRI is the gold standard for meniscal tear diagnosis, with sensitivity >90% and specificity >95% when performed with appropriate sequences. The exclusion of immediate surgical referral is appropriate, as many medial meniscus tears (especially non-displaced, horizontal, or degenerative variants) are managed conservatively—hence the emphasis on functional assessment and PT *pending MRI*. No red flags (e.g., locking, giving-way, persistent effusion, systemic symptoms) suggest instability or concomitant pathology requiring urgent intervention.
